note.subject: science

mustKnow: Conductors have free electrons; insulators do not
Electron flow is from − round to +; conventional current is from + round to −
The long thin line of a cell is the positive terminal
Cells in a row add when they face the same way; a reversed cell is subtracted
Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel across the component

notOnThisSpec: Diodes: the symbol, its one-way behaviour and its graph (not on CCEA's 2.3.4 chart)
Static electricity and charging by friction
Potential difference as the required word (CCEA says voltage)

mustBeAbleTo: Explain the difference between conductors and insulators using free electrons
Classify a material, or part of an object, as a conductor or an insulator
State that current in a metal is a flow of electrons, from negative round to positive
State that conventional current flows from positive round to negative, the opposite way
Mark the positive and negative terminals of a cell from its symbol
Add the voltages of cells in a row, subtracting any cell turned the other way round
Draw and recognise the nine circuit symbols on CCEA's chart: switch, cell, battery, resistor, variable resistor, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter and lamp
Say what a switch or an insulator does to a series circuit and to one branch of a parallel circuit
Connect an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component it tests
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks at Foundation and 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Circuit basics come early in the paper as one-mark parts: a sentence to complete with free electrons, a symbol to draw or name, the polarity of a cell, an arrow for each direction, the total of some cells in a row. Higher Tier folds the symbols into a practical circuit, inserting the lamp, meter and variable resistor symbols into gaps. Unit 7 Physics Booklet B asks for meter symbols in the right positions in a practical circuit, a mark each.
traps: Marking the long thin line as negative, or drawing electron flow and conventional current the same way round (Summer 2025 P2 Foundation Q4)
Writing battery for a single cell, or cell for two joined together (Summer 2025 P2 Foundation Q4)
Drawing a switch or a plain resistor where the variable resistor belongs (Summer 2025 P2 Higher Q9)
Taking the fuse for a resistor, drawing a line inside the resistor's box, or drawing the variable resistor's arrow corner to corner or without its head (Summer 2023 P2 Foundation Q5)
Adding the voltage of a cell that is turned round: two equal cells facing each other give 0 V (Summer 2023 P2 Foundation Q5)
Leaving out the ammeter and voltmeter symbols, or putting them in each other's places (Summer 2025 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2, Foundation)
Connecting the voltmeter in series instead of across the component (Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2, Foundation; Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q3, Higher)
Calling the plastic covering the conductor: judge by free electrons, not by which part of the object you are looking at (Summer 2023 U7 Physics Booklet B Q1, Foundation)

noteBlocks.lede: Copper carries a current and its plastic sleeve does not, because only copper has free electrons. Then the language of circuit diagrams: nine symbols, which end of a cell is positive, which way current goes, and where the ammeter and voltmeter go.
can: Explain why metals conduct and plastics insulate, using free electrons
Recognise and draw CCEA's nine circuit symbols, including the variable resistor and the fuse

noteBlocks.md: Strip a charger cable: copper inside, a plastic sleeve outside. The copper carries the current; the plastic keeps it off your fingers.

noteBlocks.alt: Two magnified views. In copper, circles for atoms each marked plus, with electrons drifting freely in the gaps between them; in plastic, every electron sits against its own atom.
noteBlocks.caption: Only the copper has electrons that are free to move.

noteBlocks.md: In a metal some electrons belong to no single atom. These **free electrons** can drift through the material, and a flow of them is an **electric current**. A material with free electrons is a **conductor**: copper, steel, aluminium. In plastic, rubber or glass every electron is held on its own atom, so nothing can move: an **insulator**.

noteBlocks.stem: A brass key and a nylon thread are each tested in a circuit. Which is the conductor, and why? [2]

steps.working: Brass is a metal: some of its electrons belong to no single atom, so it has free electrons and is a conductor.
steps.decision: A material conducts when it has electrons free to drift through it.

steps.working: Nylon holds every electron on its own atom: no free electrons, so it is an insulator.
steps.decision: Nothing in the nylon can move to carry a current.

steps.working: Both contain electrons, so having electrons does not decide it.
steps.decision: The near-miss: every material has electrons; only free ones make a conductor.

noteBlocks.prompt: A silver spoon and a porcelain cup are each tested in a circuit. Which one has free electrons?
options: the silver spoon
the porcelain cup
both, because every material contains electrons
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of the See it, a metal has electrons that belong to no single atom and can drift through it: free electrons. Silver is a metal, so the spoon has them; porcelain holds every electron on its own atom, like the nylon.

optionNotes.option: the porcelain cup
optionNotes.why: Porcelain is an insulator: every electron is held on its own atom, so none is free to move.

optionNotes.option: both, because every material contains electrons
optionNotes.why: Every material has electrons, as step 3 of the See it says; only a metal has free ones that can move.

twin.prompt: A cotton thread and a gold ring are each tested in a circuit. Which one has no free electrons?
options: the cotton thread
the gold ring
neither, because both contain electrons
twin.explain: Cotton holds every electron on its own atom, so it has no free electrons and is an insulator; gold is a metal, with free electrons.

optionNotes.option: the gold ring
optionNotes.why: Gold is a metal, so it has free electrons and conducts; the cotton is the one without them.

optionNotes.option: neither, because both contain electrons
optionNotes.why: Both contain electrons, but only the metal has free ones; the cotton's are all held on their atoms.

noteBlocks.caption: Long line positive, short thick line negative. The rest of the topic hangs on this.

noteBlocks.md: A **cell** is drawn as two parallel lines. The **long thin line is the positive terminal (+)** and the **short thick line is the negative terminal (−)**. Which end is which is the cell's **polarity**.

Two or more cells joined together make a **battery**. Their voltages add only when every cell faces the same way. Turn one round and it pushes against the others: it takes its voltage away instead of adding it.

noteBlocks.stem: Four 1.2 V cells are joined in a row, but the third one is turned round. Calculate the total voltage. [2]

steps.working: Three cells face the same way: $3 \times 1.2 = 3.6$ V
steps.decision: Add the cells that push together.

steps.working: The reversed cell pushes against them: $3.6 - 1.2 = 2.4$ V
steps.decision: Take the reversed cell's voltage away.

steps.working: Not 3.6 V: the reversed cell does not just drop out; it cancels one of the others.
steps.decision: The near-miss: a cell turned round is still in the row, pushing the other way.

noteBlocks.prompt: Three cells are joined in a row: two 2.0 V cells facing one way and a 2.5 V cell facing the other. What is the total voltage, in volts?
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of the See it, add the cells that face the same way, then take the reversed one away: 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 V, and 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 V.

twin.prompt: Six 1.2 V cells are joined in a row, and one of them is turned round. What is the total voltage, in volts?
twin.explain: Five cells push together, 5 × 1.2 = 6.0 V, and the reversed one takes 1.2 V away: 6.0 − 1.2 = 4.8 V.

noteBlocks.md: In a metal wire the current is really **electrons moving from the negative terminal round to the positive**: **electron flow**, the dashed arrows. Before electrons were discovered, scientists agreed to draw current **from positive to negative**: **conventional current**, the solid arrows. An arrow on a circuit diagram means conventional current unless told otherwise.

noteBlocks.title: Why keep a direction we know is backwards?
noteBlocks.md: The convention came first, and the rules for magnetic fields and motors were written with it, so it stays.

noteBlocks.stem: In the figure the cell sits on the bottom wire. Which terminal is positive, and which way do the conventional current and the electrons go round? [3]

steps.working: The long thin line is on the right, so the right-hand terminal is +.
steps.decision: Fix the polarity first: both directions depend on it.

steps.working: Conventional current leaves + on the right, goes up the right-hand wire, along the top through the lamp and back into − on the left: the solid arrows.
steps.decision: Conventional current runs from + to −, wherever the cell is drawn.

steps.working: The electrons go the other way round, out of − and back into +: the dashed arrows.
steps.decision: Electrons are negative, so the negative terminal pushes them out.

noteBlocks.task: Build one loop from a battery, a switch and a light bulb. Close the switch and watch the electrons move, then note which terminal of the battery they leave. Switch the current display to conventional current and see the arrows turn round. Finally change the view to the schematic one, so each part is drawn as the symbol from section 5.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a circuit with one cell and a lamp, which way do the electrons move through the wires?
options: from the negative terminal, round the circuit, to the positive terminal
from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal
out of both terminals at once, meeting at the lamp
noteBlocks.answer: from the negative terminal, round the circuit, to the positive terminal
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 3 of the See it, electrons are negative, so they are pushed out of the negative terminal and drawn round to the positive one: the dashed arrows. Conventional current, the solid arrows, is drawn from positive to negative.

optionNotes.option: from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal
optionNotes.why: That is conventional current, the direction drawn on diagrams; the electrons themselves move the opposite way.

optionNotes.option: out of both terminals at once, meeting at the lamp
optionNotes.why: Charge goes round the loop in one direction; nothing meets at the lamp, which the same current passes through.

twin.prompt: In a circuit with one cell and a buzzer, which way is the conventional current drawn round the wires?
options: from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal
from the negative terminal, round the circuit, to the positive terminal
from the buzzer back to both terminals
twin.answer: from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal
twin.explain: Conventional current is drawn from + round to −, the solid arrows in step 2 of the See it; it is the electrons that go the other way.

optionNotes.option: from the negative terminal, round the circuit, to the positive terminal
optionNotes.why: That is the electrons' direction; conventional current is drawn the opposite way, from + to −.

optionNotes.option: from the buzzer back to both terminals
optionNotes.why: The current goes round one loop in one direction; it does not split back towards both terminals.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cell sits on the right-hand wire of a circuit, drawn upright with its long thin line at the top. In which direction does conventional current leave the cell?
options: upwards, out of the top terminal
downwards, out of the bottom terminal
it depends on where the lamp is
noteBlocks.answer: upwards, out of the top terminal
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of the See it, find the long thin line first. Here it is at the top, so the top terminal is positive, and conventional current always leaves the positive terminal: upwards, out of the top terminal.

optionNotes.option: downwards, out of the bottom terminal
optionNotes.why: That would be right with the long thin line at the bottom, as in the See it; here it is at the top, so the top terminal is positive.

optionNotes.option: it depends on where the lamp is
optionNotes.why: The lamp's place changes nothing: conventional current leaves the long thin line, wherever the cell is drawn.

twin.prompt: A cell sits on the left-hand wire of a circuit, drawn upright with its long thin line at the top. In which direction do the electrons leave the cell?
options: downwards, out of the bottom terminal
upwards, out of the top terminal
it depends on where the lamp is
twin.answer: downwards, out of the bottom terminal
twin.explain: The long thin line at the top is +, so the bottom terminal is −, and electrons leave the negative terminal: downwards, as the electrons left P in step 3 of the See it.

optionNotes.option: upwards, out of the top terminal
optionNotes.why: That is the conventional current, out of the long thin line; the electrons leave the short thick line at the bottom.

optionNotes.option: it depends on where the lamp is
optionNotes.why: Only the cell's polarity matters: electrons always leave the negative terminal.

noteBlocks.md: A circuit diagram draws every part as an agreed symbol, joined by straight lines with square corners. Three rectangles cause most of the trouble.

A **resistor** is a plain rectangle. A **fuse** has a **line running through it** along its length. A **variable resistor** has an **arrow drawn across it at a slant**, and the arrowhead is part of the symbol.

noteBlocks.title: The symbol that costs marks
noteBlocks.md: Summer 2025 Higher: a switch or a plain resistor was often drawn where the **variable resistor** belonged.

noteBlocks.stem: On a circuit diagram you meet a rectangle with an arrow drawn across it at a slant. Name the component. [1]

steps.working: It is a rectangle, so it is one of the three rectangle symbols on the chart.
steps.decision: The rectangle narrows the choice; the mark on it decides.

steps.working: The arrow across it at a slant settles it: a variable resistor.
steps.decision: The arrowhead is part of the symbol: leave it off and the mark is lost.

steps.working: Without the arrow, the plain rectangle would be a resistor.
steps.decision: The near-miss: the arrow is what makes the resistance variable.

noteBlocks.prompt: On a circuit diagram, a rectangle with a straight line running through it along its length stands for which component?
options: a fuse
a resistor
a variable resistor
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of the See it, the rectangle narrows it to three and the mark on it decides: a slanted arrow for a variable resistor, nothing for a resistor, and a line running through along its length for a fuse. So this is a fuse.

optionNotes.option: a resistor
optionNotes.why: A resistor is the plain rectangle, with nothing on it; the line along its length makes this one a fuse.

optionNotes.option: a variable resistor
optionNotes.why: A variable resistor has an arrow across it at a slant; a straight line along the length is a fuse.

twin.prompt: On a circuit diagram, a rectangle with nothing drawn on it or across it stands for which component?
options: a resistor
a fuse
a variable resistor
twin.explain: The plain rectangle is a resistor; a line through it would make a fuse, and a slanted arrow a variable resistor.

optionNotes.option: a fuse
optionNotes.why: A fuse has a line running through it along its length; this rectangle has nothing on it.

optionNotes.option: a variable resistor
optionNotes.why: A variable resistor needs the slanted arrow across it; without it the rectangle is a plain resistor.

noteBlocks.caption: The nylon breaks branch A and nothing else.

noteBlocks.md: A current flows only round a **complete loop of conductors**. A **switch** is a gap you can close: closed, it completes the loop; open, it breaks the loop and everything in it stops.

In a **series** circuit one insulator or one open switch stops the whole circuit. In a **parallel** circuit each branch is its own route: on the figure the nylon stops branch A only, and lamp B stays lit.

noteBlocks.stem: In the figure the switch is closed. Explain which lamps light, and what would happen if the nylon rod were in a single loop with both lamps. [3]

steps.working: Nylon is an insulator, with no free electrons, so branch A is broken and lamp A stays off.
steps.decision: A branch with an insulator in it is not a complete route.

steps.working: Aluminium is a metal with free electrons, so branch B is a complete route of its own and lamp B lights.
steps.decision: Each parallel branch works on its own.

steps.working: In a single loop the nylon would break the only route, and both lamps would go out.
steps.decision: In series there is one route, so one break stops everything.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cell, a closed switch and two lamps are joined in one loop, with a wooden lolly stick clipped into the loop. What happens?
options: neither lamp lights, because the wood breaks the only loop
the lamp nearer the cell lights and the other does not
both lamps light, but dimly
noteBlocks.answer: neither lamp lights, because the wood breaks the only loop
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 3 of the See it, a series circuit has one route, and an insulator anywhere in it breaks that route. Wood has no free electrons, so no current flows and neither lamp lights.

optionNotes.option: the lamp nearer the cell lights and the other does not
optionNotes.why: A break anywhere in a single loop stops the current everywhere, next to the cell as well.

optionNotes.option: both lamps light, but dimly
optionNotes.why: No current crosses an insulator at all, so the lamps cannot light, not even dimly.

twin.prompt: A cell, a closed switch and a buzzer are joined in one loop, with an aluminium strip clipped into it. Does the buzzer sound?
options: yes: aluminium has free electrons, so the loop is complete
no: only copper wire can carry the current
no: the strip breaks the loop like an open switch
twin.answer: yes: aluminium has free electrons, so the loop is complete
twin.explain: Aluminium is a metal with free electrons, a conductor, as in step 2 of the See it: the loop is complete and the buzzer sounds.

optionNotes.option: no: only copper wire can carry the current
optionNotes.why: Every metal has free electrons, so every metal conducts; copper is only the most common one in wires.

optionNotes.option: no: the strip breaks the loop like an open switch
optionNotes.why: Only an insulator breaks a loop; aluminium is a conductor, so it completes it.

noteBlocks.text: 7. Where the ammeter and voltmeter go

noteBlocks.caption: The ammeter is part of the loop; the voltmeter reaches round the lamp.

noteBlocks.md: An **ammeter** measures the current through a component, so the same current has to pass through the ammeter: it goes **in series**, in the loop.
A **voltmeter** measures the voltage across a component by comparing its two ends, so it sits on its own branch from one end of the component to the other: it goes **in parallel**.

noteBlocks.stem: A pupil wants the current through a heater coil and the voltage across it. Where do the ammeter and the voltmeter go? [2]

steps.working: The ammeter goes into the loop beside the heater: in series.
steps.decision: The current it reads must pass through it, so it is part of the loop.

steps.working: The voltmeter is joined to the wire on either side of the heater: in parallel, across it.
steps.decision: It compares the two ends of the heater, so it reaches round it on a branch of its own.

steps.working: Swapped round, the voltmeter in the loop would all but stop the current, and the readings would be useless.
steps.decision: The near-miss: a voltmeter never goes in series.

noteBlocks.title: Components, symbols and measurements in circuits
noteBlocks.why: Every symbol on the CCEA list drawn and named, with the ammeter and the voltmeter put in their places. It says potential difference where CCEA says voltage, and it does not cover conventional current against electron flow, which sections 3 and 4 teach; symbols beyond CCEA's nine, such as the diode, are not examined here.

noteBlocks.prompt: A voltmeter is used to measure the voltage across a lamp. How is it connected?
options: in parallel, on its own branch from one side of the lamp to the other
in series, in the loop next to the lamp
in series, next to the cell
noteBlocks.answer: in parallel, on its own branch from one side of the lamp to the other
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 2 of the See it, a voltmeter compares the two ends of the component, so it reaches round it on a branch of its own: in parallel, across the lamp. A voltmeter drawn in series is the slip Unit 7 examiners reported in Summer 2024.

optionNotes.option: in series, in the loop next to the lamp
optionNotes.why: In the loop it would compare nothing across the lamp and would all but stop the current; a voltmeter always goes across.

optionNotes.option: in series, next to the cell
optionNotes.why: Anywhere in the loop is still in series; the voltmeter must reach from one side of the lamp to the other.

twin.prompt: A voltmeter is used to measure the voltage across a heater. Where are its two leads joined?
options: one to each side of the heater
both to the same side of the heater
into the loop, in place of a wire
twin.answer: one to each side of the heater
twin.explain: A voltmeter compares the two ends of the heater, so one lead goes to each side of it: in parallel, as in step 2 of the See it.

optionNotes.option: both to the same side of the heater
optionNotes.why: Both leads on one side compare a point with itself and read nothing; they must reach round the heater.

optionNotes.option: into the loop, in place of a wire
optionNotes.why: That puts the voltmeter in series; it must sit across the heater on its own branch.

noteBlocks.prompt: An ammeter is added to a circuit to measure the current through a lamp. Where does it go?
options: in series with the lamp, in the same loop
in parallel with the lamp, on its own branch
across the cell's two terminals
noteBlocks.answer: in series with the lamp, in the same loop
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of the See it, the reading has to be the current that goes through the lamp, so that same current must go through the ammeter: it sits in the same loop, in series. On a branch of its own it would measure something else.

optionNotes.option: in parallel with the lamp, on its own branch
optionNotes.why: That is where a voltmeter goes. An ammeter must have the lamp's current passing through it, so it goes in the loop.

optionNotes.option: across the cell's two terminals
optionNotes.why: Across the cell it is not in the lamp's loop at all; the lamp's current must pass through the ammeter.

twin.prompt: An ammeter is added to measure the current through a buzzer. Where does it go?
options: in series with the buzzer, in the same loop
across the buzzer, on its own branch
across the cell's two terminals
twin.answer: in series with the buzzer, in the same loop
twin.explain: The buzzer's current must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in the same loop, in series, as in step 1 of the See it.

optionNotes.option: across the buzzer, on its own branch
optionNotes.why: Across the buzzer is the voltmeter's place; the ammeter needs the buzzer's current to pass through it.

optionNotes.option: across the cell's two terminals
optionNotes.why: Across the cell the ammeter is out of the buzzer's loop; put it in series with the buzzer.

**Names and symbols in a table** (Summer 2023 and 2026 Foundation), or symbols drawn into a circuit's gaps (Summer 2025 Higher).

noteBlocks.stem: In the figure, write the battery's polarity in the box above it, and draw the arrows for the electron flow and the conventional current in the other two boxes. [3]

steps.working: The long thin line is at the right-hand end: write + in the box above it.
steps.decision: Polarity first: both arrows depend on it.

steps.working: Conventional current leaves + to the right, runs down the right-hand wire and comes back along the bottom, so on the bottom wire its arrow points left.
steps.decision: Conventional current runs from + round to −.

steps.working: Electrons go the other way round: on the left-hand wire, beside the lamp, their arrow points down.
steps.decision: Electrons run from − round to +.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question shows a battery with an empty box beside it for its polarity, and two more boxes for the arrows of electron flow and conventional current. What should you do first?
options: find the long thin line and mark that end +
draw the electron-flow arrow clockwise
draw both arrows pointing the same way
noteBlocks.answer: find the long thin line and mark that end +
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of the See it, both arrows depend on which end is positive, so fix that first: the long thin line is +. Then conventional current leaves the + end and electron flow goes the opposite way, so the two arrows always point in opposite directions.

optionNotes.option: draw the electron-flow arrow clockwise
optionNotes.why: Clockwise is right only for some cells: the way round depends on which end is +, so polarity comes first.

optionNotes.option: draw both arrows pointing the same way
optionNotes.why: The two arrows always point opposite ways: conventional current leaves +, electrons leave −.

twin.prompt: A question shows a cell turned on its side with its terminals unlabelled, and asks which way conventional current leaves it. What do you look for first?
options: the long thin line, which is the positive terminal
the lamp, because current flows towards it
the shorter wire, because current takes the shortest route
twin.answer: the long thin line, which is the positive terminal
twin.explain: Conventional current leaves the positive terminal, so find the long thin line first, as in step 1 of the See it; the rest follows from it.

optionNotes.option: the lamp, because current flows towards it
optionNotes.why: The current goes round the whole loop; where the lamp sits does not set its direction.

optionNotes.option: the shorter wire, because current takes the shortest route
optionNotes.why: In one loop the current has one route; its direction is set by the cell's polarity alone.

noteBlocks.md:
Explain conductors and insulators using the words free electrons.
Mark a cell's terminals, and add or cancel the voltages of cells in a row.
Draw electron flow from − to + and conventional current from + to −.
Recognise and draw all nine symbols, telling the three rectangles apart.
Connect an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component.

Circuit questions come early in P2 and pay a mark for each symbol, terminal or arrow. The first mark is usually free electrons or a symbol drawn in a gap; the last is often a direction arrow or naming a component from its symbol. Stuck on a direction? Mark the long line + first: conventional current leaves it and electrons go the other way. Write cell, not battery, for one cell.

figure.alt: A circuit with a cell standing upright on the left-hand wire and a lamp on the right-hand wire; the cell's top terminal is lettered X and its bottom terminal Y.

steps.working: The long thin line is at the bottom, so Y is the positive terminal and X is the negative terminal.
steps.decision: Fix the polarity first. Both arrows depend on it, so a wrong terminal here would cost every mark after it.

options: Because the long thin line of a cell symbol is always the positive terminal
Because the negative terminal is always drawn at the top
Because current always flows downwards through a cell
whyMenu.explain: The long thin line is positive wherever the cell is drawn, upright, sideways or upside down. Summer 2025 examiners found the negative terminal was one of the marks most often lost.

steps.working: Conventional current leaves the positive terminal Y and goes round the circuit to X: down the left wire, along the bottom, up past the lamp and back along the top.
steps.decision: Conventional current runs from + to −, whichever way up the diagram is.

options.text: it leaves terminal Y and returns to terminal X
options.feedback: Right: out of the positive terminal, back into the negative one.

options.text: it leaves terminal X and returns to terminal Y
options.feedback: That is the electrons' route. Conventional current leaves the positive terminal, Y.

steps.working: Electron flow is the opposite: out of X, along the top, down past the lamp, along the bottom and back into Y.
steps.decision: Electrons are negative, so they are pushed out of the negative terminal and drawn round to the positive one.

options.text: they leave terminal X and return to terminal Y
options.feedback: Right: electrons leave the negative terminal, X.

options.text: they leave terminal Y and return to terminal X
options.feedback: That is conventional current. Electrons leave the negative terminal, X, and go the other way.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: X is negative. Conventional current flows from Y round the circuit to X; electrons flow from X round to Y.

twin.stem: A cell is drawn on the top wire of a circuit with its long thin line on the right. Which way does conventional current leave the cell? [1]

options.text: to the right, out of the right-hand terminal
options.feedback: Right. The long thin line on the right is the positive terminal, and conventional current leaves it.

options.text: to the left, out of the left-hand terminal
options.feedback: The left-hand terminal is the short thick line, the negative terminal. Conventional current leaves the positive one.

workedExamples.stem:
A torch holds four 1.5 V cells in a row. The last one has been put in the wrong way round.
Calculate the total voltage. [2]

steps.working: Three of the four cells face the same way; the last one faces the other way.
steps.decision: Check each cell's long line before adding anything: polarity decides whether a cell adds or subtracts.

options: Because a cell turned round pushes against the others instead of with them
Because a cell turned round stops working altogether
Because only the first cell in a row counts
whyMenu.explain: A reversed cell still pushes; it just pushes the other way. That is why two equal cells facing each other give zero, the fact Summer 2023 examiners found only the most able candidates knew.

steps.working: Three cells facing the same way: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 V
steps.decision: Add the cells that push together.

steps.working: The reversed cell pushes against them: 4.5 − 1.5 = 3.0 V
steps.decision: Take the reversed cell's voltage away. It does not just drop out: it cancels one of the others.

steps.working: Plastic is an insulator: it has no free electrons, so no current can pass through the plastic block.
steps.decision: Name each block's material type first, with its reason: that is what the conductor-or-insulator word is for.

options: Because a current needs free electrons to move through a material
Because plastic is too thick for the current
Because the plastic is further from the cell
whyMenu.explain: Current in a solid is free electrons drifting. Plastic holds every electron on its atom, so nothing can flow through it, however thin it is or wherever it sits.

options.text: the plastic block is an insulator
options.feedback: Right: no free electrons.

options.text: the plastic block is a conductor
options.feedback: Plastic has no free electrons, so it is an insulator.

steps.working: Branch A is broken by the insulator, so lamp A does not light.
steps.decision: A branch with an insulator in it is not a complete route.

options.feedback: Right: its branch is not a complete route.
No current at all passes the plastic, so lamp A cannot light, not even dimly.

steps.working: Copper is a conductor with free electrons, and branch B is its own complete route across the cell, so lamp B lights.
steps.decision: Each parallel branch works on its own: the broken branch A does not stop branch B.

options.text: lamp B lights, because branch B is complete
options.feedback: Right: a conductor completes branch B, and branch A's gap does not affect it.

options.text: lamp B stays off, because branch A is broken
options.feedback: That would be true in series. In parallel each branch is its own route, so branch B still works.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Lamp A stays off: plastic is an insulator, with no free electrons, so branch A is broken. Lamp B lights: copper is a conductor, and branch B is a complete route of its own.

items.stem: Before we start: what are the small negatively charged particles in every atom, found outside the nucleus?

options.feedback: Electrons. This whole topic is about what they can and cannot do.
Protons are positive and sit in the nucleus. The negative particles outside it are electrons.
Neutrons have no charge and sit in the nucleus. The negative particles outside it are electrons.

items.stem: Before we start: a lamp is joined to a cell by two wires, but one wire has come unclipped. Does the lamp light?
items.skill: Prerequisite: a circuit must be a complete loop

options.text: no, because the circuit is no longer a complete loop
options.feedback: No. A current needs a complete loop from one terminal of the cell back to the other.

options.text: yes, because one wire is enough to carry the current to the lamp
options.feedback: A current has to go round and come back. With one wire unclipped there is a gap, so nothing flows.

options.text: yes, but more dimly than before
options.feedback: There is no half-way: with a gap in the loop no current flows at all, so the lamp is off.

items.stem: Before we start: which of these is the unit of voltage?

options.feedback: The volt. You will add cells' voltages in volts in this topic.
The amp is the unit of current. Voltage is measured in volts.
The ohm is the unit of resistance. Voltage is measured in volts.

items.stem: A cable has a copper core inside a plastic covering. Which part is the conductor, and why?
items.skill: Conductors and insulators by free electrons

options.text: the copper core, because it has free electrons
options.feedback: Right. The copper has free electrons; the plastic covering has none.

options.text: the plastic covering, because it surrounds the current
options.feedback: The covering is there because it is an insulator: it has no free electrons. The copper core carries the current.

options.text: both parts, because every material contains electrons
options.feedback: Every material has electrons, but only a conductor has free ones. The plastic's electrons are held on their atoms.

items.stem: On the symbol for a cell, which line is the negative terminal?

options.feedback: Right. Short thick line negative, long thin line positive.
The long thin line is the positive terminal. The short thick line is negative.

options.text: either line, depending on which way the current is drawn
options.feedback: Polarity is fixed by the symbol, not by the arrows: the arrows are drawn from it. The short thick line is always negative.

items.stem: Conventional current in a circuit flows …

options.text: from the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal
options.feedback: Right. Electrons go the other way, from negative round to positive.

options.text: from the negative terminal, round the circuit, to the positive terminal
options.feedback: That is electron flow. Conventional current was fixed before electrons were known, and it runs from positive to negative.

options.text: in the same direction as the electrons
options.feedback: The two go opposite ways round the loop. Conventional current runs from positive to negative; electrons from negative to positive.

items.stem: Two 1.5 V cells are joined in a row facing each other, positive to positive. What is their total voltage?
items.skill: Cells in a row with one reversed

options.feedback: Right. They push against each other equally, so they cancel.
That adds them as if both faced the same way. Facing each other, they push in opposite directions and cancel.
That counts one cell and ignores the other. The second cell is still there, pushing back, so the two cancel.

items.stem: Which description is the symbol for a variable resistor?

options.text: a rectangle with an arrow drawn across it at a slant
options.feedback: Right. The slanted arrow, head included, is what makes it variable.

options.text: a rectangle with a straight line running through it along its length
options.feedback: That is a fuse. A variable resistor has an arrow across it at a slant.
A plain rectangle is a fixed resistor. The variable resistor has a slanted arrow across it.

items.stem: An ammeter and a voltmeter are used to test a lamp. How should they be connected?

options.text: the ammeter in series with the lamp, the voltmeter in parallel across it
options.feedback: Right. The ammeter shares the lamp's current; the voltmeter compares the lamp's two ends.

options.text: the ammeter in parallel across the lamp, the voltmeter in series with it
options.feedback: Those are swapped. The ammeter goes in the loop and the voltmeter goes across the lamp.

options.text: both meters in series with the lamp
options.feedback: The ammeter belongs in series, but a voltmeter in series gives no useful reading. It goes across the lamp.

parts.stem: Which circuit, A, B, C or D, has both meters connected correctly for testing the lamp?

options.feedback: In A the two meters have swapped places: the voltmeter is in the loop and the ammeter is across the lamp.
In B the voltmeter is in the loop, in series. A voltmeter has to go across the lamp, on its own branch.
Right. The ammeter is in the loop, in series, and the voltmeter is across the lamp, in parallel.
In D the voltmeter is across the cell, not the lamp, and the ammeter is across the lamp instead of in the loop.

hints: Look for the ammeter in the loop and the voltmeter reaching round the lamp.
parts.workedSolution: C. Its ammeter is in the loop, so the lamp's current passes through it, and its voltmeter is on its own branch across the lamp.

parts.stem: Explain why the ammeter must be connected in series with the lamp.

accepted: The same current that passes through the lamp must also pass through the ammeter.

any: current through the lamp also passes through the ammeter
current must pass through the ammeter
current must flow through the ammeter
all the current passes through it
all the current flows through it

scheme.for: the (same) current that flows through the lamp must flow through the ammeter

hints: What does an ammeter measure, and what has to happen to that current for the ammeter to see it?
parts.workedSolution: The same current that passes through the lamp must also pass through the ammeter, so the ammeter has to be in the same loop.

parts.stem: Explain why the voltmeter must be connected across the lamp.

accepted: A voltmeter compares the two ends of the lamp, so it must be joined to either side of the lamp.

any: compares the two ends of the lamp

scheme.for: it measures the voltage across the lamp / compares the two ends of the lamp

hints: A voltmeter compares two points. Which two points matter for the lamp?
parts.workedSolution: A voltmeter compares the two ends of the lamp, so it must be joined to either side of the lamp, on its own branch.

commonErrors.feedback: A voltmeter goes in parallel, on its own branch across the lamp. It is the ammeter that goes in series.

parts.stem: Switch S1 is closed and switch S2 is left open. Which lamps light?

options.feedback: Right. S1 completes the main line; S2 is open, so the branch with lamp X is broken, but lamp Y's branch is complete.
Lamp X's branch still has S2 in it, and S2 is open. That branch is broken, so only lamp Y lights.
An open switch breaks only the branch it sits in. S2 is in lamp X's branch, so lamp Y still has a complete route.
S2, the open switch, sits in lamp X's own branch, so lamp X is the one that stays off.

hints: Trace each branch. Is every part of it a closed path?
parts.workedSolution: Lamp Y only. S1 is closed, so the main line is complete. S2 is open, which breaks the branch with lamp X; lamp Y's branch has no switch, so it is complete.

parts.stem: Which switch turns both lamps off at once?

options.feedback: Right. S1 is in the main line, which carries the current for both branches.
S2 sits in lamp X's branch only. Opening it leaves lamp Y's branch complete.

hints: Which switch does every current pass through?
parts.workedSolution: S1. It is in the main line, so every current in the circuit passes through it; opening it breaks the circuit for both branches.

parts.stem:
The torch holds three 1.5 V cells in a row, all facing the same way.
Calculate the total voltage of the three cells.
hints: Cells facing the same way add.
parts.workedSolution: All three face the same way, so their voltages add: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 V.

parts.stem:
The middle cell is taken out and put back the wrong way round.
Calculate the new total voltage.
hints: The reversed cell does not just stop helping: it pushes the other way.
parts.workedSolution: Two cells still face the same way and give 3.0 V; the reversed cell pushes against them with 1.5 V. Total: 3.0 − 1.5 = 1.5 V.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds all three. The middle cell is the wrong way round, so its voltage is taken away.
That is the total with the reversed cell removed. It is still in the torch, pushing the other way, so subtract its voltage as well.
One reversed cell cancels one forward cell, not all of them. One cell's worth is left.

parts.stem: State the name for two or more cells joined together.
hints: It is the everyday word people use, wrongly, for a single cell.
parts.workedSolution: A battery. One cell on its own is a cell; two or more joined together make a battery.

commonErrors.feedback: One on its own is a cell. Two or more cells joined together make a battery.

parts.stem:
The spring that presses on the cells is made of metal.
Explain why it must be made of a metal.

accepted: Metal is a conductor: it has free electrons, so the current can pass through the spring.

scheme.for: metal is a conductor / has free electrons (so current can pass through the spring)

hints: The spring is part of the loop. What must every part of the loop do?
parts.workedSolution: Metal is a conductor: it has free electrons, so the current can pass through the spring and the loop is complete.

parts.stem: Explain why the lamp lights only when the switch is closed.

accepted: Closing the switch completes the circuit, so a current can flow through the lamp.
When the switch is closed the circuit is complete, so current flows.

scheme.for: closing the switch completes the circuit
so a current can flow (through the lamp)

hints: Say what the switch does to the loop, then what that allows.
parts.workedSolution: Closing the switch completes the circuit, so a current can flow round the loop and through the lamp. When it is open there is a gap and no current flows.

parts.stem:
The meter in the circuit shows whether a current is flowing, even when the current is too small to light the lamp.
Name this meter.
hints: It measures current, and it is in the loop.
parts.workedSolution: An ammeter. It measures the current, and it sits in the loop in series with the sample.

commonErrors.feedback: A voltmeter measures voltage and sits across a component. The meter in the loop that shows the current is an ammeter.

parts.stem: Use the table to decide which two materials are insulators.

options.feedback: Right. Both gave a current of 0.00 A: no charge flowed through them.
Copper and steel gave the largest currents: they are the conductors. Insulators let no current through, so look for the readings of zero.
Pencil lead is not a metal, but it gave a current of 0.24 A, so it conducts. The readings of zero belong to glass and dry wood.

hints: An insulator lets no current through. Look for the readings of zero.
parts.workedSolution: Glass and dry wood. Both gave a current of 0.00 A, so no charge flowed through them.

parts.stem:
Pencil lead is graphite, which is not a metal.
Suggest why graphite conducts electricity.

accepted: Graphite has free electrons that can move through it.

scheme.for: it has free (delocalised) electrons that can move

hints: Whatever conducts must have one particular kind of electron.
parts.workedSolution: Graphite has free (delocalised) electrons that can move through it, just as a metal has, so it can carry a current.

parts.stem: Put the steps of the method in the right order.

expectedOrder: Connect the cell, the switch, the lamp, the ammeter and the two crocodile clips in one loop.
Clip a sample of the first material between the two crocodile clips.
Close the switch and read the ammeter.
Open the switch, then clip in the next material.

scheme.for: circuit built and sample clipped in before the switch is closed
reading taken with the switch closed, and the switch opened before the next material

hints: Build first, then test, then change the sample with the circuit switched off.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Connect the cell, the switch, the lamp, the ammeter and the two crocodile clips in one loop. 2. Clip a sample of the first material between the two crocodile clips. 3. Close the switch and read the ammeter. 4. Open the switch, then clip in the next material.

parts.stem: The student also wants to measure the voltage across the sample. How should the voltmeter be connected?

options.text: to the two crocodile clips, in parallel with the sample
options.feedback: Right. A voltmeter goes across the component it measures, on its own branch.

options.text: in the loop, in series between the cell and the lamp
options.feedback: A voltmeter in series is the slip examiners keep seeing. It belongs across the sample, joined to either side of it.
That would measure the cell's voltage, not the voltage across the sample. Join it to either side of the sample.

scheme.for: in parallel with the sample (across the crocodile clips)

hints: A voltmeter always reaches from one end of the thing it measures to the other.
parts.workedSolution: Across the two crocodile clips, in parallel with the sample, so it compares the two ends of the sample.

context.setting: A torch taken apart: three cells, a metal spring and strips, a switch, a lamp and a plastic case

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: the cells face the same way, positive of one against negative of the next, so their voltages add
a cell put in the wrong way round pushes against the others, so the total voltage falls
the metal spring and strips are conductors because they have free electrons
the plastic case is an insulator: its electrons are held on their atoms, so it carries no current
closing the switch completes the circuit so a current flows; opening it breaks the circuit
electrons flow from the negative terminal round the circuit to the positive terminal
conventional current is drawn from the positive terminal round to the negative terminal

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point is counted only once it is explained, not just named: 'the spring conducts' needs 'because it has free electrons' to earn the conductor point. The two directions are two separate points, and an answer that gives them the same way round earns neither.

hints: Take the bullet points in order and give each one a because.
parts.workedSolution: The three cells must face the same way, with the positive terminal of each against the negative terminal of the next, so that their voltages add. If one cell is put in the wrong way round it pushes against the others and the total voltage drops, so the lamp is dimmer. The metal spring and strips are conductors because metals have free electrons that can move through them. The plastic case is an insulator: its electrons are held on their atoms, so no current passes through it and it is safe to hold. Closing the switch completes the circuit, so a current flows through the lamp; opening it leaves a gap and the current stops. In the wires the electrons flow from the negative terminal of the battery, round the circuit, to the positive terminal. Conventional current is drawn the opposite way, from the positive terminal round to the negative terminal.

context.setting: A battery of 6 cells of 1.5 V, some of them turned round

parts.stem:
A battery is made of 6 cells, each 1.5 V, joined in a row. Some of the cells have been put in the wrong way round, and the battery's total voltage is 3.0 V.
Calculate how many cells are turned round.

scheme.for: each reversed cell cancels one forward cell: (forward − reversed) × 1.5 = 3.0, with forward + reversed = 6

hints: A reversed cell does not just drop out: it cancels one of the forward cells.
parts.workedSolution: Each reversed cell cancels a forward cell, so the total is (forward − reversed) × 1.5 V. For 3.0 V that difference is 2, and forward + reversed = 6, so 4 face forward and 2 are reversed: (4 − 2) × 1.5 = 3.0 V.

commonErrors.feedback: That treats the reversed cells as if they had been taken out, so only two cells seem to be working. A reversed cell pushes against a forward one: with 4 forward and 2 reversed, (4 − 2) × 1.5 = 3.0 V, so 2 are reversed.

parts.stem: One more of the forward cells is turned round. Calculate the new total voltage of the battery.
hints: Now three face each way.
parts.workedSolution: Three face forward and three are reversed, so they cancel in pairs: (3 − 3) × 1.5 = 0.0 V.

commonErrors.feedback: That leaves the reversed cells out instead of subtracting them. Three push one way and three the other, so they cancel: 0.0 V.
That adds all six cells as if they faced the same way. Three are reversed and cancel the other three: 0.0 V.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'A torch holds four 1.5 V cells in a row, but the last one has been put in the wrong way round. Calculate the total voltage. [2]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Three cells face the right way: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 V
The reversed cell does nothing, so total = 4.5 + 0
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: A cell turned round does not do nothing: it pushes the other way with its full 1.5 V. So it is taken away, not left out: 4.5 − 1.5 = 3.0 V.
correction: Three cells face the right way: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 V
The reversed cell pushes against them: 4.5 − 1.5
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of two: the three forward cells are added correctly. The second mark needs the reversed cell subtracted, because it is still in the torch and still pushing, just the wrong way.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciaran is asked: 'A cell is drawn with its long thin line on the left. In which direction does conventional current leave the cell? [2]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The long thin line is the positive terminal, so the left terminal is positive
Conventional current flows from the negative terminal to the positive terminal
So conventional current leaves the cell from the right-hand terminal
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 describes electron flow. Conventional current is the older convention: it flows from the positive terminal round to the negative one, so it leaves by the long thin line, on the left. The electrons are the ones that leave the negative, right-hand terminal.
correction: Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal
So conventional current leaves the cell from the left-hand terminal
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of two: the positive terminal is right. The direction mark needs conventional current from + to −, leaving on the left. Summer 2025 Foundation examiners found few candidates got the terminal and both directions right.

prompts.prompt: What does a conductor have that an insulator does not?
prompts.answer: Free electrons: electrons that are not held by one atom and can move through the material. An insulator's electrons are all held on their atoms.

prompts.prompt: In a metal wire, which way do the electrons move round a circuit?
prompts.answer: From the negative terminal, round the circuit, to the positive terminal.

prompts.prompt: Which way does conventional current flow round a circuit?
prompts.answer: From the positive terminal, round the circuit, to the negative terminal: the opposite way to the electrons.

prompts.prompt: What is the difference between a cell and a battery?
prompts.answer: A battery is two or more cells joined together; one cell on its own is a cell.

prompts.prompt: Where are an ammeter and a voltmeter connected when they test a lamp?
prompts.answer: The ammeter in series, in the loop with the lamp; the voltmeter in parallel, across the lamp.

prompts.prompt: Two 1.5 V cells are joined facing each other. What is the total voltage, and why?
prompts.answer: 0 V: they push in opposite directions and cancel.

prompts.prompt: How do the symbols for a resistor, a fuse and a variable resistor differ?
prompts.answer: Resistor plain; fuse has a line through; variable resistor, a slanted arrow.
